title: Sleep Staging Is Not Guesswork

reading.body:
Oura marketed its smart ring as achieving 95% accuracy in sleep staging comparable to clinical sleep labs. The lawsuit alleges the device lacks the physiological sensors needed for this measurement, instead relying on AI estimates from heart rate and temperature data without the brain activity electrodes that clinical labs use. A system deployed to consumers with claims it could not meet represents a failure to validate performance before release.

The company disputes this, stating its sleep staging was validated in peer-reviewed studies and performs favorably against polysomnography. It is not established whether Oura's marketing claims exceeded what its validation studies actually showed, or whether the company understood the limitations of its sensors when making those claims. The dispute turns on what "comparable to clinical sleep labs" means when applied to a consumer device using fundamentally different measurement methods.

reports.title: Oura, Smart Ring Maker, Sued for Alleged False Claims and Unreliable AI
Oura faces lawsuit accusing it of misleading consumers about sleep-tracking accuracy

summary:
Oura, a smart ring company valued at $11 billion, faces a class-action lawsuit filed by Clarkson Law Firm for allegedly making false advertising claims about its product. The suit alleges that Oura Ring devices, which cost $300 and up, cannot accurately track sleep stages as advertised. According to the lawsuit, the rings' algorithms and sensors lack the capability to detect the physiological signals necessary for precise sleep measurement, relying instead on unreliable AI-generated estimates comparable to guessing. The company markets its rings as having 95% sleep staging accuracy comparable to clinical sleep labs, but sleep labs require multiple electrodes to measure brain activity that Oura devices do not possess.

Oura responded by defending its technology, stating that its sleep staging has been validated in peer-reviewed studies and compared favorably against polysomnography, the medical standard. The company emphasized that while Oura Ring estimates sleep stages using multiple physiological signals like heart rate and temperature, it is not a medical device or substitute for clinical sleep studies. It remains unclear what compensation affected buyers could receive if the lawsuit succeeds. This marks the second major lawsuit against Oura, following a previous class action alleging the company collected personal information without customer consent.
